\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{شيد} (shayyada)}{شيد (shayyada)}]{\ar{شيد} (shayyada) — to erect, to build up}

\label{lesson:AR-C331-shayyada}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for a shackle, then the Arabic for to release.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{شيد}}
\textbf{\ar{شيد}} — \emph{shayyada} — \textquotedblleft{}to erect, to build up\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{شيد} \ar{الملك} \ar{قصرا} \ar{كبيرا}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{shayyada al-malik qaṣran kabīran.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The king built a great palace.
\end{quote}

Present: \ar{يشيد}, \emph{yushayyid}.

Of grand buildings; \ar{بنى} is the everyday verb.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{شيد}} (\emph{shayyada}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{sh-y-d} (Lane), where \emph{shīd} is plaster and Form II \emph{shayyada} is \textquotedblleft{}to plaster a building, to raise it high\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling what happened.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{shayyada}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{shayyada}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{shayyada al-malik qaṣran kabīran.} — The king built a great palace.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for a shackle, then the Arabic for to release, then say \emph{shayyada} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ar{شيد} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To erect, to build up\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{سيطر} (sayṭara)}{سيطر (sayṭara)}]{\ar{سيطر} (sayṭara) — to control, to take control}

\label{lesson:AR-C331-saytara}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for to release, then the Arabic for to erect.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{سيطر}}
\textbf{\ar{سيطر}} — \emph{sayṭara} — \textquotedblleft{}to control, to take control\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{سيطر} \ar{رجال} \ar{الإطفاء} \ar{على} \ar{الحريق}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{sayṭara rijāl al-iṭfāʾ ʿalā al-ḥarīq.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The firefighters brought the fire under control.
\end{quote}

Present: \ar{يسيطر}, \emph{yusayṭir}.

It takes \ar{على}: \ar{سيطر} \ar{على}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{سيطر}} (\emph{sayṭara}) is filed under the root \emph{s-ṭ-r} (Lane), the root of \emph{saṭr}, a line, with \emph{muṣayṭir}, an overseer. Its earlier history, perhaps through Aramaic, is not settled.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling what happened.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sayṭara}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sayṭara}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sayṭara rijāl al-iṭfāʾ ʿalā al-ḥarīq.} — The firefighters brought the fire under control.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for to release, then the Arabic for to erect, then say \emph{sayṭara} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ar{سيطر} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To control, to take control\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{امتد} (imtadda)}{امتد (imtadda)}]{\ar{امتد} (imtadda) — to extend, to stretch}

\label{lesson:AR-C331-imtadda}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for to erect, then the Arabic for to control.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{امتد}}
\textbf{\ar{امتد}} — \emph{imtadda} — \textquotedblleft{}to extend, to stretch\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{امتدت} \ar{الحديقة} \ar{حتى} \ar{النهر}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{imtaddat al-ḥadīqa ḥattā an-nahr.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The garden stretched as far as the river.
\end{quote}

Present: \ar{يمتد}, \emph{yamtadd}.

Of time too: \ar{امتد} \ar{الاجتماع} \ar{ساعتين}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{امتد}} (\emph{imtadda}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{m-d-d} (Lane), \textquotedblleft{}to stretch out\textquotedblright{}. It is Form VIII, \textquotedblleft{}to be stretched, to reach\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling what happened.
\end{grammarlens}

\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{imtadda}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{imtaddat al-ḥadīqa ḥattā an-nahr.} — The garden stretched as far as the river.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for to erect, then the Arabic for to control, then say \emph{imtadda} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ar{امتد} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To extend, to stretch\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{ازدهر} (izdahara)}{ازدهر (izdahara)}]{\ar{ازدهر} (izdahara) — to flourish, to thrive}

\label{lesson:AR-C331-izdahara}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for to control, then the Arabic for to extend.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{ازدهر}}
\textbf{\ar{ازدهر}} — \emph{izdahara} — \textquotedblleft{}to flourish, to thrive\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{ازدهرت} \ar{التجارة} \ar{في} \ar{المدينة}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{izdaharat at-tijāra fī al-madīna.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Trade flourished in the city.
\end{quote}

Present: \ar{يزدهر}, \emph{yazdahir}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{ازدهر}} (\emph{izdahara}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{z-h-r} (Lane), \textquotedblleft{}to shine; to blossom\textquotedblright{}, the root of \emph{zahra}, a flower. It is Form VIII, where the \emph{t} turns to \emph{d} after \emph{z}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling what happened.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{izdahara}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{izdaharat at-tijāra fī al-madīna.} — Trade flourished in the city.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for to control, then the Arabic for to extend, then say \emph{izdahara} again
\end{itemize}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{إمبراطور} (imbarāṭūr)}{إمبراطور (imbarāṭūr)}]{\ar{إمبراطور} (imbarāṭūr) — an emperor}

\label{lesson:AR-C331-imbaratur}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for to extend, then the Arabic for to flourish.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{إمبراطور}}
\textbf{\ar{إمبراطور}} — \emph{imbarāṭūr} — \textquotedblleft{}an emperor\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{حكم} \ar{الإمبراطور} \ar{بلادا} \ar{واسعة}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{ḥakama al-imbarāṭūr bilādan wāsiʿa.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The emperor ruled wide lands.
\end{quote}

An empire is \ar{إمبراطورية}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{إمبراطور}} (\emph{imbarāṭūr}) is usually traced to Latin \emph{imperator}, \textquotedblleft{}a commander\textquotedblright{}, which reached Arabic through a European language.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling what happened.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for to extend, then the Arabic for to flourish, then say \emph{imbarāṭūr} again
